sources.text:
The EU’s 28th State?
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floats making Canada the bloc’s first associate member.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca.
The EU Looks Across the Pond
Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member.
Welcome back to World Brief, where we’re looking at Canada’s future with the European Union, a war crimes conviction against former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci, and alleged Houthi targeting of the holy city of Mecca.
The EU Looks Across the Pond
Could the European Union expand beyond Europe? Some experts argue that being part of the continent is an integral component of membership. But that is the proposal European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen floated on Wednesday, when she suggested making Canada the bloc’s first associate member.
“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney seated on her left, von der Leyen outlined what such a future might look like, starting with an expansion of their existing free-trade agreement.
Carney has been pitching such an arrangement to European officials for months. A Canadian official told The Associated Press last week that the two sides are discussing potential ties that stop just short of full membership. This could include allowing Canadian citizens to live and work in EU member states without needing a visa. An expanded partnership might also bolster collaboration in defense production, critical minerals procurement, economic security, and the development of artificial intelligence, among others.
Canada wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc, Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said on Wednesday, adding that further discussions are expected to take place at the Canada-EU summit in October. Under EU regulations, the bloc requires unanimous approval to welcome new members.
Although von der Leyen insisted on Wednesday that the Canada proposal is “not a partnership against anyone else,” the gesture comes at a time when both Canada’s and Europe’s relations with the United States under President Donald Trump are greatly strained.
Last month, the White House imposed sweeping tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting “dollar for dollar” retaliatory duties on around 700 U.S. products. This was in spite of Canada being one of the United States’ largest trading partners; bilateral trade accounted for around $872.3 billion in 2025. Alongside a recent war of words between Trump and Ontario Premier Doug Ford as well as the U.S. president’s repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state, Ottawa has begun to prioritize its relationship with the EU over what it once considered its closest partner.
But not everyone in Europe appears thrilled with von der Leyen’s proposal. “Of all the third countries, Canada is one of the few that we all want to get closer to right now,” an EU diplomat told the Financial Times. “But even with them, we all know we have to be careful when you start talking about trade access and preferential treatment.” Notably, 10 EU member states have yet to ratify the bloc’s 2017 free-trade deal with Canada, citing several provisions that they argue favor Canadian investors.
Whether the idea ever materializes, the fact that it’s being talked about at such high levels is a sign of what Carney called the “rupture in the world order.” The Canadian premier will take the stage on Thursday to address the European Parliament.
Today’s Most Read
- Trump Is Killing ‘Strategic Ambiguity’ Over Taiwan by James Crabtree
- Why My Kyiv Visit Worried Me So Much by Ravi Agrawal
- Only China, India, and Russia Can End the Iran War by Amir Handjani
What We’re Following
Guilty of war crimes. Former Kosovar President Hashim Thaci was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Wednesday after being found guilty of orchestrating war crimes during the country’s brutal fight for independence against Serbia in the late 1990s. He continues to deny any wrongdoing and is expected to appeal the ruling.
The sentence was handed down by the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, a special tribunal at The Hague. According to the tribunal, Thaci oversaw the murder, torture, arbitrary detention, and abuse of alleged opponents, including ethnic minorities and perceived collaborators, while serving as the top commander of the since-disbanded Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA). “The vast majority of them were innocent civilians,” the tribunal said of Thaci’s victims. Thaci was sentenced alongside three other senior members of the ethnic Albanian KLA.
Wednesday’s ruling is expected to heighten divisions between Serbians and Kosovar Albanians, the latter of whom often regard Thaci as a hero for his contribution to Kosovo’s independence. Clashes broke out between Thaci supporters and security at The Hague when protesters tried to walk to the tribunal. Incumbent Kosovar Prime Minister Albin Kurti condemned Wednesday’s ruling, saying, “While the verdict may have been formally pronounced in the name of the people of Kosovo, this hollow formula must not be conflated with the will of the people.”
Mecca is under fire. Saudi forces claimed on Wednesday local time to have intercepted a Houthi drone targeting the holy Muslim city of Mecca the day before. According to Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen, the attempted attack crossed a “red line,” as it was “intended to provoke the feelings of millions of Muslims.” The Organization of Islamic Cooperation similarly denounced the operation as a “heinous” assault.
This is the first alleged Houthi strike aimed at Mecca since fighting erupted between the Iranian proxy group and Saudi-backed forces in July. The Houthis denied Riyadh’s allegations, with rebel spokesperson Hazem al-Assad saying, “The claims about targeting Mecca are a worn-out lie that has been used before and no longer fools anyone.”
Both sides have escalated their assaults in recent days. On Wednesday, Saudi warplanes struck Yemeni territory, and Houthi troops attacked Red Sea port cities and Saudi military bases. Such assaults have exacerbated the already tenuous global energy crisis and injected further insecurity into the war-embroiled Middle East.
Seeking peace. Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo resumed peace talks in Geneva on Wednesday, alongside mediators from Qatar, Togo, and the United States. The two-day session—the seventh meeting since the two countries signed a U.S.-brokered peace accord last year—aims to address continued fighting in eastern Congo between Congolese forces and Rwanda-backed M23 rebels.
Less than a year ago, Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi and Rwandan President Paul Kagame signed an agreement in Washington to end the deadly conflict. However, without M23 representatives in attendance—and Kigali maintaining that it does not support the rebel group despite U.N. evidence to the contrary—Trump’s self-proclaimed “historic” peace deal did little to actually quell the fighting; just days after the December 2025 signing, around 200,000 people fled renewed violence in the region.
Since then, the situation in eastern Congo has continued to deteriorate despite repeated cease-fire attempts. During this week’s talks, Kigali is expected to seek assurances that armed groups will not be allowed to operate in Congolese territory, while Kinshasa asserts that foreign security forces have no right to Congolese soil.
Odds and Ends
A Paris court awarded Kim Kardashian 1 euro (or $1.15) on Tuesday as compensation for being the victim of an armed robbery in 2016. Kardashian was at the Hôtel de Pourtalès for Paris Fashion Week when a gang of eight thieves, six of whom are currently in their 60s or 70s, bound the media personality with zip ties and stole more than $6 million in jewelry; the so-called grandpa robbers were found guilty of armed robbery and kidnapping, among other charges, last year. Kardashian has since described the incident as “the most terrifying experience of my life” but only requested a symbolic 1 euro in restitution.

sources.news_title: EU Opens Opportunity for Canadian Membership
sources.text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen suggested the European Union may open its doors for Canada to join as an “associate member.”
Addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen stated, “I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU. We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world. And we will now build our shared future as well – thank you for being here.”
She also stated that Carney’s presence at the event stood as a “symbol of the enduring friendship between our people. Our cultural, historical and personal links run deep within the fabric of our societies.”
Von der Leyen went on to declare that the European Union will create an Alliance for the Future alongside Canada for “common prosperity and economic security space.
“We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project. We will work on energy, critical minerals and batteries. On AI, quantum, cyber and economic security,” she explained, declaring that the EU seeks to “bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”
The offer comes as Canada seeks to move away from its trade relations with the United States amid ongoing tariff battles. Last month, President Trump announced his plan to implement stronger tariffs on some Canadian products beginning in January 2027.

EU chief wants Canada to become an 'associate member'. What does that mean?
EU-CANADA/MEMBERSHIP (CORRECTED, EXPLAINER):CORRECTED-EXPLAINER-EU chief wants Canada to become an 'associate member'. What does that mean?
By Julia Payne
BRUSSELS, Sept 16 - European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the European Union's first "associate member".
Earlier this week, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney — who was in Strasbourg to listen to von der Leyen's annual State of the Union address — said Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU but not membership.
WHAT MIGHT THE NEW RELATIONSHIP INVOLVE?
There is currently no such status as "associate member" set out in the European Union's treaties — though various versions of an associate-type of membership have been floated in the bloc over the years.
Most recently, Germany suggested Ukraine be an associate member as an interim stage to full accession, though the proposal failed to gain traction as some EU capitals pushed back.
WHAT IS CANADA SEEKING?
Carney is seeking new alliances amid repeated threats by U.S. President Donald Trump against Canada's sovereignty.
Both sides want to forge deeper cooperation to counter U.S. and Chinese economic dominance as well as preserve democracy and the rules-based international order, which they see as under threat.
In her speech, von der Leyen said the two sides would create a "common prosperity and economic space". This would include joint work on manufacturing, a tech alliance, integration of defence industrial bases, the Arctic, AI, energy and critical minerals.
WHY MIGHT THE IDEA OF 'ASSOCIATE MEMBER' BE COMPLICATED?
Implementing such an 'associate' status would be unprecedented and may be legally complex.
Von der Leyen was speaking in her capacity as President of the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm. It would fall on the EU member states to decide whether the idea flies.
There is no suggestion von der Leyen is proposing enshrining the status of 'associate member' in EU treaties. That would require unanimity among all 27 capitals and ratification by all domestically.
Canada and the EU already have a trade agreement, called CETA. More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.
If Canada wishes to become locked into the EU's Single Market, Ottawa would need to reconcile Canada's norms and regulations to match EU law.
Canada would become a rule-taker with no say on policy if it entered the Single Market without full membership like Iceland, Norway, and Liechtenstein who are members of the European Economic Area.
Switzerland has select access to the Single Market through trade agreements including the free movement of people, transport and product standards recognition.
Canada's rules have historically been geared towards its biggest trade partner, the United States.
WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR EU CANDIDATE COUNTRIES?
The quest for a deeper alliance between Canada and the EU will not impact the path to accession for European candidate states but it may serve as an irritant if Canada is perceived to be getting special treatment.
Accession negotiations and aligning with EU norms is a long process that often requires candidate nations to push through politically sensitive reform.
Full membership can only be granted to European states and provides access to the bloc's €18 trillion Single Market, voting and representation, EU funding and legal recourse to the European Court of Justice.
Ukraine saw Germany's proposal for "associate membership" as "unfair" as Kyiv would participate but with no voting rights.
The EU has said it could admit new members as soon as 2030. Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova are the most advanced among candidate countries.

sources.news_title: EU proposes Canada become the bloc’s first ‘associate member’
sources.text:
EU proposes Canada become the bloc’s first ‘associate member’
BRUSSELS — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Canada becoming the first associate member of the European Union, forging a novel transatlantic alliance as President Donald Trump tears apart the old one.
She offered the invitation during her state of the union address in Strasbourg, France, Wednesday, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance.
“In this new world, we must urgently reimagine our partnerships and build global coalitions for our resilience and democracies,” von der Leyen said. “I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the European Union.”
By creating a tailor-made title just for Canada, the E.U. is sending a powerful signal as a trading bloc that it can expand beyond its borders and reinvent itself in the aftermath of Brexit, when it lost an economic powerhouse. What this means in practice is another matter, with negotiations likely to take years. Significantly, it also suggests a path for the U.K. to re-stitch its ties with the E.U., though with Canada ahead in terms of establishing what associate membership will entail.
Regular membership of the E.U. entails a lengthy accession process and comes with rights, like access to the single market, as well as financial, fiscal and legal obligations. There is no precedent for associate membership, and proposals earlier this year to offer a “membership light” to Ukraine faced backlash from many member states.
Certain countries like Iceland, Norway, Liechtenstein and Switzerland, however, have special arrangements with the bloc on topics such as the free movement of goods and people. Iceland two weeks ago rejected reopening talks with the E.U. over full membership.
Carney warned earlier this year that the “rules-based international order” was effectively dead and has made repeated calls for so-called middle powers to band together to oppose the pressure tactics and intimidation of the world’s dominant economies. Bloomberg reported earlier that the transatlantic allies were in talks to forge a new alliance to ensure their security.
Von der Leyen also discussed closer cooperation with Canada on manufacturing, tech, defense and energy, and cited the Arctic as a “flagship joint project.”
Carney’s government, economically shaken by a trade war with the U.S., has made a deeper E.U. partnership and other partners a top priority. After U.S.-Canada talks ended last month, Trump imposed 50% tariffs on $20 billion of goods imported from Canada, and Carney soon retaliated with tariffs on a roughly equal amount of U.S.-made products.
Canada’s focus is on concluding the ratification of CETA, the E.U.-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, an accord that was negotiated a decade ago but that still hasn’t been formally approved by 10 European countries, according to people familiar with the discussions.
Carney and von der Leyen held a meeting in Strasbourg. Afterward, his office said Canada seeks a “far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future” with the E.U.
“This includes critical minerals, defense industrial capacity, AI and compute, energy security, space, as well as financial services and payments,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement. “The leaders also discussed moving toward seamless digital trade in non-agricultural goods and a wide range of services.”
Outstanding issues with the bloc also include ironing out differences over E.U.’s carbon pricing tool on imported goods and its deforestation and pesticides rules.
Bloomberg reported earlier that E.U. officials see the potential to pursue a closer relationship with Canada than with the U.K. The E.U. views Canada as successfully implementing a so-called sovereignty agenda on economic and defense matters — a campaign that could inform the bloc’s own push to cut foreign dependencies. Furthermore, Canada doesn’t have the Brexit baggage London carries.
“We already are looking at how to increase the trade, what we can do in research and innovation, how we can cooperate more in defense, and also how we can support each other in all the multilateral negotiations, if it comes to WTO and other trade negotiations,” E.U. trade chief Maros Sefcovic told reporters in Strasbourg after the speech.
Sefcovic said he would meet his Canadian counterpart, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne later Wednesday.
Canada, unlike the U.K., has been granted access to SAFE, the bloc’s $173 billion loan program for defense procurement.
Canada and the E.U. will be expected to make progress ahead of their summit in Montreal in October, at which they could sign a digital trade agreement that it’s been in the works, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.
“Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” von der Leyen said. “That power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest.”

sources.news_title: Canada, the EU's first 'associate member'? Brussels says yes — Ottawa says not so fast
sources.text:
- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen used her Wednesday State of the Union speech to invite Canada to become the EU's first associate member, a status that has never existed inside the bloc and still has no legal definition.
- Prime Minister Mark Carney's office welcomed the gesture but stopped short of endorsing membership, days after a senior Canadian official dismissed a Wall Street Journal report on the idea as an overstatement of what Ottawa was actually pursuing.
- The overture follows the collapse of US-Canada trade talks and Washington's 50 percent tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian goods; the two governments are due to hash out details when they meet in Montreal on October 29-30.
A Standing Ovation Breaks With Protocol
Von der Leyen made an offer Wednesday with no real precedent in EU history. During her annual State of the Union speech in Strasbourg, the European Commission chief invited Canada to join the bloc under a brand-new label, one that doesn't currently exist anywhere in EU treaties. Carney, understood to be the first non-European government leader ever invited to sit in on the speech in person, watched from the front row as von der Leyen turned to address him directly, according to NPR. Parliament gave him a standing ovation, and he later crossed the chamber to shake her hand, a scene several outlets covering the speech described in detail. Von der Leyen tied the move to what she called a fracture in the global rules-based order, arguing that democracies now need to rethink who their partners are. She framed it as a shared project, telling Carney she wanted to work toward opening a path for Canada to become "the first associate member of the EU."
What "Associate Member" Would Even Mean
Nothing like this status exists in EU law today, and any version of it would still need sign-off from all 27 member governments, according to ABC News Australia. Canada was never eligible for full membership since it isn't a European country, so von der Leyen instead proposed retiring the current CETA trade pact in favor of something broader she dubbed the Alliance for the Future. The plan she outlined spans smart manufacturing, a shared technology partnership, tighter integration of defense industries, a flagship Arctic project, and cooperation on energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing and cybersecurity, per Global News. The stated goal, in her words, was to take the Canada relationship to its highest possible level.
In Wednesday's speech, von der Leyen put the trade increase since CETA at 75 percent over less than a decade, a figure Global News and other outlets covering her remarks repeated word for word.
Ottawa's Cooler Read on the Moment
Carney's government responded with noticeably more restraint than the applause inside the chamber suggested. A formal statement from the Prime Minister's Office, relayed by CP24, framed Wednesday's overture as an invitation to build something new together rather than a membership offer, tying any closer relationship explicitly to reinforcing Canada's own sovereignty. Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's ambassador to the EU, put it more bluntly to reporters, essentially arguing it was premature to settle on a label for an arrangement whose substance hadn't been worked out yet. That caution isn't new. Just three days before the speech, a senior Canadian government official told reporters that Ottawa wasn't pursuing EU membership in any form, calling an earlier Wall Street Journal report on the idea an overstatement of what was actually under discussion. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre pounced on that same report over the weekend, posting online that Canadians should reject any talk of joining Brussels, per CBC News: "we will NEVER be the 28th EU state."
The Trade War Behind the Pivot
The timing is no accident. Negotiations between Canadian and American trade officials fell apart in the final hours before a late-August deadline, triggering 50 percent U.S. tariffs on close to $20 billion of Canadian exports — a slice worth about 5.5% of all the goods Canada sends south each year, hitting everything from wine and dairy to furniture and hockey equipment. Carney pulled his negotiating team back to Ottawa and rejected Washington's terms outright, telling reporters plainly that "they asked too much, and they offered too little." Canada answered with matching dollar-for-dollar tariffs that took effect September 8. Washington's chief trade negotiator, Jamieson Greer, offered a competing account, according to The Week, accusing Canadian officials of backing away from commitments made earlier in the same week of talks. Close to seven in ten dollars of everything Canada sells abroad still crosses into the United States, the exact dependency Carney has said repeatedly that he wants to shrink, per NPR.
A Rocky Precedent
Recent history suggests turning Wednesday's applause into an actual agreement won't be quick. Roughly a decade after CETA was first signed, about ten EU governments, among them France, Italy, Ireland, Poland and Greece, still haven't ratified it through their own parliaments, per Global News. The idea of pulling Canada closer isn't new, either. Back in June, Finnish President Alexander Stubb floated growing the EU to as many as 40 members and named Canada alongside the U.K., Turkey, Norway and Iceland as candidates, joking — per CNBC — that he'd sooner welcome Ottawa in as member number 28 than watch it get swallowed up as Washington's 51st, a dig at Donald Trump's repeated musings about annexing Canada.
What Comes Next: Montreal
The next real test already has a date attached. The Council of the European Union has confirmed that the two governments will hold their next bilateral gathering in Montreal on October 29-30, where negotiators from both sides are expected to start filling in what an associate arrangement would actually look like on paper. For a bloc that still hasn't finished ratifying one ordinary trade agreement with Canada a decade later, turning this week's ovation into a working new status will be its own kind of test.

sources.news_title: EU and Canada pursue a values-based alliance
sources.text:
EU and Canada pursue a values-based alliance
Leaders on both sides of the Atlantic are aiming for more economic and defense sovereignty – while reimagining cooperation among like-minded democracies.
Canada clearly has no intention of allowing itself to become the United States’ 51st state. But it might be willing to consider becoming the 28th state to join the European Union. Sort of.
On Wednesday, Ursula von der Leyen, head of the European Commission, invited the U.S.’s northern neighbor to join the 27-nation bloc – the world’s third-largest economy – as an “associate member.” Her reasoning?
“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world,” Ms. von der Leyen declared. “We believe that power does not belong to the strongest, the richest or the loudest – but to all of us. That democracies have the freedom to choose with whom to work.” Such a partnership, she was careful to note, is “not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
On Thursday, Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney addresses the European Parliament, and is likely to express similar sentiments and support for closer ties.
This week’s events mark ongoing geopolitical shifts that Mr. Carney himself put into top gear in January. Speaking at the annual World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, he declared that the long-standing world order was ruptured, and urged “middle powers” to step up and build new coalitions.
As these formerly close U.S. allies seek to untether themselves from decades of dependence and redefine sovereignty, they are finding it’s important to reaffirm bedrock social and political traditions they hold in common. Articulating democratic values at this time can help reshape regional trade and defense, as well as views of national identity and international responsibility.
Canada “is an underrated military power,” according to the European Council on Foreign Relations, pointing to its experience in Arctic military strategy. And Canada’s plans to increase defense spending could mean potential business for European military contractors. Earlier this week, Mr. Carney welcomed international asset managers to a summit in Toronto, where his government showcased more than 160 multibillion-dollar investment opportunities in mining, energy, ports, manufacturing, and technology.
The EU, too, appears to be adopting more expansive views of its role. “By creating a tailor-made title just for Canada,” according to Bloomberg News, “the EU is sending a powerful signal as a trading bloc that it can expand beyond its borders and reinvent itself.”
Beyond pragmatism or realpolitik, analysts believe that the collaborative, respectful approach to partnership that the EU and Canada are pursuing could have broader, global resonance.
“The European project emerged from the ruins of the second world war,” Fabian Zuleeg, head of the European Policy Centre, wrote in The Guardian Monday. “Now, in a very different geopolitical context, we need ambitious mechanisms for bringing like-minded democracies together.”

sources.news_title: What von der Leyen and Carney are up to with Canada’s ‘associate’ EU membership
sources.text:
“We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said to Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney today. “And we will now build our shared future as well,” she added.
Her comments came during her state of the European Union speech in Strasbourg, France, which Carney attended and during which she proposed Canada become an “associate member” of the bloc. Below, our experts examine this unexpected proposal and the motivation behind it from the viewpoints of both Brussels and Ottawa.
Jörn Fleck is the senior director of the Atlantic Council’s Europe Center and a former European Parliament staffer.
Confusion over membership, but clarity on motivation
Von der Leyen’s pledge to develop ever-closer relations with Canada, including with an offer of associate membership in the EU, comes with more questions than answers. It is not unusual for these addresses to be high on rhetoric yet thin on details. But this pitch is stratospheric.
The European Union and Canada already maintain close relations. The EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA) has been provisionally in force since 2016. Canada is the first non-European country to participate in the EU’s Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, funding scheme for defense projects.
Von der Leyen is pushing for more. She wants to upgrade relations to an “Alliance for the Future,” and she ticked off a wish list of partnership ideas: intelligent manufacturing, a tech alliance, integrated defense industrial bases, a flagship project in the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum, cyber, and economic security. But the pièce de résistance was the idea of associate EU membership for Canada.
Details stop here. Cue the confusion.
First, there is no such thing as associate membership in the EU treaties. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz pitched the idea for Ukraine to be an associate member this summer as a kind of waystation to eventually become a full-fledged member. This is probably not what von der Leyen has in mind for Canada.
Second, there’s the question of how associate membership interacts with other formats for non-EU countries to engage with the bloc. Norway, Iceland, and Liechtenstein are in the EU’s single market via the European Free Trade Association (EFTA). Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and Ukraine all have their own arrangements. Reports suggest Canada could get access to the Erasumus+ student exchange program, EU-funded research grants, and a mutual recognition of workers’ qualifications. But these together hardly graduate to the ambition von der Leyen presented today.
Perhaps the EU will offer Canada some form of more advanced access to the bloc’s market. But the EU has been extremely hesitant to open parts of its cherished single market. This hesitancy is out of concern that countries should not be able to cherry-pick how integrated or not countries are with the EU. Just ask the post-Brexit Brits about their experience with that approach.
Third, there is the issue of Canada’s representation in the EU. If Ottawa more closely integrated into the European market, for instance, what say would Canada have in Brussels? Would Canada have voting rights? If not, would Canada then become a rule-taker on the many EU economic and trade rules and swap Washington’s patronizing treatment for the worst version of the Brussels effect? It seems doubtful that Canada would accept that, including its business community that is carefully watching EU rules on carbon border taxes and new steel tariffs. Never mind the opinions of some EU member states—ten of which have not even ratified the CETA yet and prevent its most promising investment provisions from entering force.
These questions aside, von der Leyen’s offer brings home just how much the Trump administration’s disengagement and disruption is reshaping geopolitics for US allies. That von der Leyen so strongly embraced Canada, which is in its own trade war with the United States, is a signal in its own right. It goes to show how much the “rupture” that Carney spoke of at Davos earlier this year is driving the psychology of leaders around the world as they try to navigate a new geopolitics for their countries.
Imran Bayoumi is a deputy director and resident fellow with the GeoStrategy Initiative in the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security.
Is this the Carney Doctrine in action?
Von der Leyen’s announcement that the European Union has invited Canada to be its first “associate member” caps off a whirlwind week for Carney. He hosted global business investors at a conference in Toronto, and the United Kingdom is considering joining the Canada-led defense, security and resilience bank (DSRB), potentially adding a major partner to the fledgling effort.
It seems to be the week when the Carney Doctrine finally took off. The vision that Carney laid out at the World Economic Forum earlier this year, where he called for middle powers to band together and resist the coercive action of the world’s hegemons, had failed to get traction. The world’s middle powers are a disparate bunch and share little in terms of worldview or strategy to approach the “rupture” in the international order that Carney spoke of. Nonetheless, Canada’s associate membership with the EU is the closest that middle powers have come to truly banding together in a more volatile world.
Still, questions remain. What exactly “associate membership” entails is unclear as no other country in the world holds that title. There are existing sore points in the relationship between Ottawa and Brussels, as well. As Jörn also notes above, ten EU member states have yet to ratify the EU-Canada trade deal from 2016.
Ultimately, for Canada, the decision to pursue closer ties with the EU is a smart one. The ongoing trade war with the United States has pushed bilateral relations to a low point and Canadians want their leaders to diversify away from Washington, with Europe as a desired partner. However, Canada’s new partnership with the EU makes a near-term resolution between Ottawa and Washington in their trade war more unlikely. Carney continues to build leverage and political will by holding out, and he is demonstrating to Canadians that alternatives exist.

sources.text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen says she wants to open the door to Canada becoming the EU's first "associate member" in a push to forge new links among allies in "an openly hostile world".
European Union MPs gave a standing ovation after she made the proposal and then walked over to embrace Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in the European Parliament to hear her annual State of the Union address.
New partnerships were needed "in the cold fragility of today's world," von der Leyen told the assembly in Strasbourg, without detailing what associate membership would mean.
The 27-nation bloc faces war at its borders, with Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Both the EU and Canada have also been facing stiff rivalry on trade and other issues from the administration of US President Donald Trump and from an increasingly assertive China.
"I said we must urgently reimagine our partnerships. So, I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen said.
The EU and Canada "see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy," von der Leyen told the assembly.
Carney welcomed von der Leyen's proposal for "a far stronger, more ambitious alliance in the future," his office said, adding: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."
He did not mention associate membership.
It will be up to EU member states, and not von der Leyen alone, whether her proposal, which left some EU watchers befuddled, goes ahead.
The EU has historically resisted flexible alliances that have no legal status. EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full accession.
One EU diplomat expressed surprise at von der Leyen's proposal, saying "nobody really knows what it means."
The diplomat added there were concerns that the European Commission chief "is overpromising and won't be able to deliver."
Carney's European trip follows the collapse of Canada-US trade talks last month, sparking a series of back-and-forth tariff measures.
He has pledged to double Canada's non-US trade in the next decade as the country pivots away from its southern neighbour amid an increasingly acrimonious trade war.
In her speech, von der Leyen said the EU and Canada will work together across sectors.
"We will work on intelligent manufacturing. We will create a tech alliance. We will integrate defence industrial bases. We will make the Arctic a flagship joint project," she said.
"Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system," she added.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Heorhii Tykhyi, said his country welcomed deeper ties between the EU and Canada and would closely watch what comes next.

sources.news_title: EU proposes Canada as its first 'associate member', a status that does not yet exist
sources.text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed on Wednesday that Canada become the European Union's first “associate member,” a status not provided for in the bloc's treaties and whose details have not been defined.
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada being the first associate member of the EU,” von der Leyen said during her annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, addressing Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, a special guest of the European Parliament seated in the front row. The proposal drew a standing ovation. Carney is due to address the chamber on Thursday.
Full membership is not on the table: Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union reserves membership for European states. The bloc has also been reluctant in the past to entertain flexible categories of membership.
Von der Leyen further proposed moving from the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, known as CETA, to what she called an “alliance for the future,” aimed at creating a common prosperity and economic security space, with cooperation on technology, critical raw materials, energy and defense. She said the Union must urgently reimagine its partnerships and stressed the initiative “is not an alliance against anyone else.”
Carney's office welcomed the proposal, saying Canada is deepening ties with the European Union to strengthen its sovereignty. Canada's ambassador-designate to the bloc, Jonathan Wilkinson, told reporters, however, that the two sides remain far from landing an agreement.
The rapprochement responds to the trade war with the United States, destination of around 70% of Canadian exports. US President Donald Trump has imposed tariffs on Canada and has repeatedly suggested the country become the 51st state, an idea Carney rejects. Canada and the European Union had already launched a strategic partnership in 2025, whose implementation they reviewed in November.
Bilateral trade in goods and services reached €130.8 billion last year, some US$151 billion, according to the European Commission, an increase of more than 80% over the past decade. The Union is Canada's second largest trading partner. CETA eliminated 99% of tariff lines when it provisionally entered into force in 2017, though ten member states have yet to ratify it.
Finland's President Alexander Stubb had set out on June 3 a vision of a Union of up to forty states including Canada, the United Kingdom, Türkiye, Norway and Iceland, asking whether it would not be preferable for Canada to be the Union's 28th state rather than the United States' 51st. In March, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot suggested Ottawa might accede at some point.
Support in Canada is not unanimous. A survey by pollster Abacus Data put backing for deeper cooperation with the bloc at around 80% and support for eventual accession at 49%; the poll does not specify sample size or margin of error. Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre called Carney's effort misplaced and said Canada will be neither the 51st state of the United States nor the 28th of the European Union.

(ZeroHedge)—Thanks to how mean President Trump has been, Canada could become the first-ever “associate member” of the European Union under a proposal unveiled Wednesday by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, as Ottawa looks to reduce its economic dependence on the United States.
Speaking during her annual State of the Union address in Strasbourg, with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in the front row as the first foreign head of government ever to attend the speech, von der Leyen said Brussels wants to take its relationship with Canada to an unprecedented level.
“We must urgently reimagine our partnerships,” von der Leyen said, before telling Carney she wanted to work with him on “opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU.”
There is just one complication: no such status currently exists.
EU treaties allow European countries to apply for full membership, while Brussels maintains an assortment of trade, association and single-market agreements with countries outside the bloc. But “associate membership” would be something new, meaning its rights, obligations and legal structure would have to be negotiated essentially from scratch.
Reuters notes that any serious move toward such a status would also face the politically difficult task of winning support from all 27 EU member states.
And Carney himself has stopped short of calling for full EU membership. On Sunday, after a Wall Street Journal report that Canada was exploring membership, he described what Ottawa is seeking as a “unique alliance” with Europe. He addresses the European Parliament on Thursday.
The substance of what Brussels is proposing, however, goes considerably beyond another trade agreement.
Canada and the EU already have CETA, their comprehensive free-trade deal. Von der Leyen said Wednesday that the two sides now want to move “from CETA to an Alliance for the Future” encompassing manufacturing, technology, defense, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and Arctic security.
“We will integrate defence industrial bases,” she said.
That process has already begun.
Canada became the first non-European country allowed to participate in the EU’s €150 billion SAFE defense procurement program under an agreement signed in February and formally concluded by the EU Council in June. The arrangement allows eligible Canadian companies and Canadian-origin products to participate in procurement financed by the program.
The EU-Canada defense relationship has also expanded into military mobility, interoperability, maritime and space security and defense-industrial cooperation.
Then there’s the economics of the idea. Roughly 70% of Canadian exports go to the United States, making any rapid decoupling unrealistic. At the same time, Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of a 51st state have given Ottawa a powerful incentive to diversify. Europe, meanwhile, needs resources.
Von der Leyen warned Wednesday that Europe remains more than 80% dependent on China for many critical raw materials, with dependence reaching 90% for some rare earths.
“No country can do this alone,” she said.
Canada possesses significant reserves of nickel, uranium, potash, cobalt, lithium and rare earth elements, among other commodities increasingly regarded as strategic inputs for batteries, semiconductors, defense equipment and energy infrastructure.
That makes a deeper Canada-EU relationship potentially complementary: Europe gets another source of strategic commodities and energy while Canada gets a large alternative market, industrial investment and greater access to European defense and technology programs.
There is nevertheless a potentially uncomfortable tradeoff for Ottawa. If “associate membership” eventually includes meaningful access to the EU’s roughly €18 trillion single market, Canada could be required to align portions of its regulatory regime with EU rules. Reuters notes that this could leave Ottawa accepting European regulations without receiving the voting rights enjoyed by actual EU members.
Canada could gain market access while becoming, at least in some areas, a rule-taker rather than a rule-maker.

sources.text:
EU chief says she wants Canada to become the bloc’s 1st associate member
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
- EU chief Ursula von der Leyen has proposed making Canada the bloc’s first associate member, expanding their trade pact into an ‘Alliance for the Future’ built on shared prosperity, security and democratic values.
- Driven by U.S. President Trump’s tariffs and talk of Canada as the 51st state, Ottawa seeks to reduce reliance on the United States, secure visa-free access to Europe and deepen economic, defense and tech ties while protecting sovereignty.
- Canada, already the first non-European participant in the European Union’s SAFE defense program, will hammer out details of the unprecedented status at an October summit, amid questions over approval and implications across the 27-nation bloc.
STRASBOURG, France — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Wednesday proposed making Canada the European Union’s first associate member, a striking overture as President Trump’s threats drive Ottawa closer to Europe.
Trump’s tariffs and repeated talk of making Canada the 51st state have soured the relationship between the North American neighbors. Canada is seeking to reduce its dependence on the United States, the destination for roughly 70% of its exports, and Prime Minister Mark Carney has called for a “unique alliance” with the EU.
In her annual State of the European Union address, Von der Leyen said Canada and the EU would build on their existing free trade agreement, known as CETA, with a broader “Alliance for the Future” aimed at creating “a common prosperity and economic security space.”
She cast that closer relationship as rooted not just in trade but in shared democratic values.
“Above all, dear Mark, Europe and Canada believe in democracy,” Von der Leyen said to Carney, who received a standing ovation at the European Parliament in Strasbourg. He is due to address the Parliament on Thursday.
Canada seeks a relationship just short of EU membership
A Canadian official familiar with the discussions said last week that Ottawa was exploring ties with the EU that could stop just short of membership. The official said Canada would seek an arrangement allowing its citizens to live and work in Europe without visas as part of a broader strategic partnership.
Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada’s ambassador-designate to the EU, said Wednesday that Ottawa had discussed associate membership with European officials before Von der Leyen’s speech and “knew that that was something that was on the table.” He said Canada had talked to the EU about the Alliance for the Future, while European officials had raised associate membership.
Wilkinson said Canada is not seeking full EU membership because it would require surrendering some sovereignty. Instead, Ottawa wants “to get as close as we possibly can” to the bloc in a way that strengthens Canadian sovereignty rather than diminishes it, he said.
Carney’s office welcomed Von der Leyen’s proposal, saying Canada was deepening ties with the EU “to strengthen our sovereignty” and supported a move beyond CETA.
Canada has already joined the EU’s defense procurement program
Von der Leyen said the expanded partnership would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, defense production, the Arctic, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity and economic security.
“This is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength,” she said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”
Because Canada joining the EU as an associate member would be a first, there is no rule book on how that would work or what it would mean in practice. It is unclear who would need to approve membership, and how long that could take.
Wilkinson said Ottawa and Brussels are deliberately focusing first on the substance of the relationship rather than what to call it. “Before you actually get to the point where you decide what you’re going to call something, you should actually know the shape,” he said.
He said the shape is likely to become clearer at the Canada-EU summit in October, when the two sides expect to make an announcement and may settle on how to describe it.
Currently, all steps toward EU membership must be approved unanimously by the 27 member countries.
The idea of associate membership has been floated in the past for Ukraine, or for post-Brexit Britain, but no concrete steps have been taken.
Beyond trade: Canada and EU explore a broader alliance
The relationship between Canada and the European Union has reached a point where the two sides need to move beyond rhetoric and start building something more substantive, said Tobias Cremer, a German member of the European Parliament.
“Now is the time to stop sending each other love letters and put meat on the bone,” said Cremer, from the center-left Social Democrats.
He argued that any new arrangement should be more ambitious than another trade or defense agreement, describing the goal as a more holistic strategic alliance between Canada and the EU.
Existing frameworks such as CETA could provide a foundation, Cremer said, but should be used more fully and expanded. The case for closer ties, he said, is increasingly being driven by geopolitics as much as economics.
The aim, he said, should ultimately be bigger than a bilateral arrangement — potentially positioning the EU as a convener of middle powers, an idea Carney has also raised.
Canada this year became the first non-European country to join the EU’s $173-billion SAFE defense program, giving Canadian companies access to joint procurement as Europe seeks to increase its defense readiness.
Iratxe García Pérez, president of the Socialists & Democrats group in the European Parliament, praised Carney for showing “great courage confronting Donald Trump” and said allies were needed to defend “sovereignty, solidarity and international law.”
Carney said Tuesday that economic integration, once viewed largely as an asset, is increasingly “being used as a weapon by certain countries.” Discussions will ramp up at the Canada-EU summit in late October, he said.
Trump rupture accelerates Canada’s turn toward Europe
Canada has retaliated against U.S. tariffs and rejected trade terms Carney says would weaken its sovereignty.
The EU has taken a different course with Washington, reaching a trade agreement that set a 15% U.S. tariff ceiling on the vast majority of EU exports while Europe eliminated tariffs on U.S. industrial goods.
That contrast has loomed over Carney’s push for closer European ties. In a closely watched speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, in January, he urged middle powers to work together to increase their leverage in an era of great-power rivalry.
“When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered,” Carney said.
“This is not sovereignty,” he added. “It is the performance of sovereignty while accepting subordination.”
Carney’s Davos speech drew a personal rebuke from Trump, and Von der Leyen’s overture to America’s neighbor could raise the temperature again.
Gillies writes for the Associated Press. AP writer Sam McNeil in Brussels contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: EU head tells Carney she wants Canada as bloc's first 'associate member'
sources.text:
STRASBOURG, FRANCE — European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Wednesday she wants Canada to become the first "associate member" of the European Union, though Canadian officials downplayed the significance of that term.
Prime Minister Mark Carney listened in the front row as von der Leyen laid out key pillars for stronger co-operation between Europe and Canada in her state of the union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France.
She said the two sides must "urgently reimagine" their partnership and move beyond a free-trade agreement to bring the relationship to the "highest level possible."
"I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to be the first associate member of the EU," von der Leyen said, drawing a standing ovation from most members in the chamber.
Carney nodded, rose from his seat, approached von der Leyen and embraced her. He briefly waved to the chamber before returning to his seat.
Carney is set to address the European Parliament on Thursday at the invitation of European Parliament President Roberta Metsola.
"We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world," von der Leyen said. "And we will now build our shared future as well."
Carney is in France this week to secure a stronger alliance with Europe focused primarily on trade, defence and people-to-people ties — the latest move in his campaign to reduce Canada's reliance on the United States.
But Jonathan Wilkinson, Canada's incoming ambassador to the European Union, suggested the term "associate membership" isn't yet firm.
Speaking to reporters after von der Leyen's speech, Wilkinson said the two sides have been talking about how to define an enhanced partnership but they're still "a ways away" from finding the term to describe it.
"What we're focused on is actually driving results in the specific sectors that we're actually focused on. Eventually we will get to the issue of what's the best way to describe it," Wilkinson said in Strasbourg.
"You've heard Prime Minister Carney describe it as an 'alliance of the future,' you heard that from President von der Leyen. You've heard her also mention the idea of associate membership. We're not there. It's an opportunity for us to talk about that, but we're really much more focused on getting concrete results."
Wilkinson said details of the partnership are expected to be announced at the Canada-EU Summit in Montreal this October. He sidestepped questions about whether he knew in advance von der Leyen was going to invite Canada to be an associate member in her address.
He said Canada is not looking to become a full member of the European Union "because that is a sovereignty issue," but is instead looking to get as close as possible with European partners without sacrificing self-determination.
"We certainly had conversations about that beforehand," Wilkinson said. "We knew that was going to be on the table. We talked to them about 'alliance for the future,' which she used."
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly told reporters Wednesday in Toronto that talks with Brussels are aimed at a "very ambitious level" of collaboration that gives Canada more options in an age of protectionism.
She said that could include ensuring Canada is not cut out of steel and aluminum trade with Europe if it acts to protect its industries from foreign tariffs. She did not specifically call out U.S. tariffs, which have hit European steel and aluminum exports as well.
"We want to make sure that markets are still opened between us, and that not only our free trade-agreement holds, but that we align our industrial policies, particularly in sectors impacted by the tariffs," she said.
Joly also said the new arrangement could provide "greater market integration" as allies work to meet NATO's spending target and protect digital sovereignty and children's safety online.
The Wall Street Journal, citing sources, first reported last week that Canada was exploring membership in the EU. Carney threw cold water on that report.
Speaking to reporters during the Toronto International Film Festival, he said Canada was not looking to become a member of the European Union but rather was seeking a "unique alliance" with the economic bloc.
Carney received a red-carpet reception earlier Wednesday at the European Parliament building, where he was greeted by Metsola and von der Leyen.
There was applause as he entered the chamber and he received a standing ovation from many parliamentarians after Metsola formally introduced him.
"Mark, your presence here is a symbol of the enduring friendship between our people," von der Leyen said in her address, which lasted more than an hour. "Our cultural, historical and personal links run deep within the fabric of our societies.
"We see the world with the same eyes, from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains."
In her speech, von der Leyen said Europe and Canada would move from a free-trade agreement to "an alliance for the future," while deepening co-operation on the Arctic, energy, critical minerals and batteries.
In a statement, the Prime Minister's Office didn't offer any clarity on associate member status but rather focused on von der Leyen's other remarks about forming a partnership.
Carney was not made available to take questions from reporters Wednesday.
"We welcome President von der Leyen's proposal that Canada and the European Union move beyond the (free trade agreement) to an alliance for the future," a spokesperson from his office said.
"This is a unique, positive approach that we will define together."
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre criticized Carney for not being straightforward with Canadians on what he is pursuing with Brussels, and warned Ottawa could lose control on matters such as immigration.
"Canadians are not pawns on a global chessboard. They deserve to be masters in their own homes," he said at a caucus retreat in Penticton, B.C.
"Canada must be independent and sovereign."
Carney stayed in the chamber for more than an hour after von der Leyen's address, listening to speeches from other political party leaders.
Terry Reintke, leader of the Greens in the European Parliament — which has seven per cent of the seats — began her remarks by quipping that she hopes to see Carney in the chamber in the future.
"You're very welcome in this house. And I hope you're already feeling comfortable among the member states sitting here because we hope to see you there very often," Reintke said.
Ireland's Minister of State for European Affairs Thomas Byrne sat beside Carney throughout the morning.
He began his speech reflecting on their ancestry, as their respective grandfathers came from the same county in Ireland.
"Your presence here today is a visible reflection of the deep bond shared by the European Union and Canada," Byrne said.
"Thank you, President von der Leyen. Your proposal significantly advances the relationships between the European Union and our great friend, Canada."
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Sept. 16, 2026.
— With files from Dylan Robertson in Ottawa and Sandra Ezekwesili in Toronto
Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

sources.news_title: EU Chief Proposes Canada As Bloc's First 'Associate Member' - American Liberty News
sources.text:
Ursula von der Leyen’s unprecedented proposal could deepen trade, defense, and technology ties, but “associate membership” has no established definition and no agreement has been negotiated.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen proposed Wednesday that Canada become the European Union’s first “associate member,” offering Prime Minister Mark Carney a potentially historic partnership that would stop short of full membership.
“I would like to work with you on opening the door for Canada to being the first associate member of the European Union,” von der Leyen said during her annual State of the European Union address in Strasbourg, France.
Carney, seated in the European Parliament chamber, nodded, rose, embraced von der Leyen, and kissed her on both cheeks as lawmakers delivered a standing ovation.
The public exchange marked a significant diplomatic opening, but it did not create a new membership status or bind either side to an agreement. The EU treaties do not currently establish “associate membership” as a defined category, and von der Leyen offered few details about the rights, obligations, or approval process involved.
Canada would not become a voting member of EU institutions under the proposal as presently described. It also remains unclear whether Canadians would receive broader rights to live and work in Europe or whether Canadian companies would gain access to parts of the EU single market.
The two sides are expected to explore those questions before a Canada-EU summit scheduled for late October in Montreal.
Von der Leyen calls for ‘alliance for the future’
Von der Leyen unveiled the idea while Carney attended her address as an invited guest.
“We will move from CETA to an alliance for the future, to create a common prosperity and economic security space,” she said, referring to the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement between Canada and the EU.
The proposed alliance would cover advanced manufacturing, technology, energy, critical minerals, batteries, artificial intelligence, quantum computing, cybersecurity, Arctic policy, and defense production.
“This is not a partnership against anyone else, but for our common strength,” von der Leyen said. “In short, we want to bring the relationship with Canada to the highest level possible.”
Her remarks can be viewed in the European Commission’s official video and transcript.
Von der Leyen said trade in goods between Canada and the EU has grown by 75% since CETA took effect provisionally in 2017. The agreement eliminated most tariffs and expanded commercial access, but it has not been fully ratified by every EU member state.
That unfinished process demonstrates one obstacle facing a more ambitious arrangement. Depending on its terms, an associate agreement could require approval from EU governments, the European Parliament, Canada, and potentially national or regional legislatures across Europe.
What ‘associate member’ could mean
The phrase does not carry an agreed legal meaning within the EU.
Several European countries maintain close relationships with the bloc without being members. Norway and Iceland participate in the European Economic Area, giving them extensive access to the single market while requiring them to follow many EU rules. Switzerland relies on a series of bilateral agreements. Turkey has a customs union with the bloc, while other nations have association agreements tailored to trade and political cooperation.
None is formally called an associate member.
Canada’s arrangement would therefore have to be designed from the ground up or constructed by expanding existing agreements. The final package could range from a largely symbolic strategic partnership to substantial integration in selected economic, defense, and mobility programs.
Canadian officials have explored an arrangement under which citizens could live, work, and study in Europe without obtaining traditional visas. Such mobility rights would require extensive negotiations and were not granted by Wednesday’s announcement.
Full EU membership is a separate matter. Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union says any “European state” may apply to join, creating an obvious geographic and legal obstacle for Canada. Full accession would also require Canada to transfer substantial regulatory and political authority to EU institutions, an outcome Carney has not sought.
Carney welcomes deeper partnership
Carney’s office welcomed von der Leyen’s initiative and said closer EU ties would strengthen Canadian sovereignty.
The prime minister has described his objective as a “unique alliance,” rather than conventional EU membership. Earlier in the week, he played down reports that Canada was looking to join the bloc outright.
Canada is seeking to reduce its economic dependence on the United States, which receives roughly 70% of Canadian exports. Relations between Ottawa and Washington have deteriorated amid tariffs, retaliatory measures, and President Donald Trump’s repeated statements about Canada becoming the 51st state.
Carney has rejected trade terms that he says would undermine Canadian sovereignty. At the World Economic Forum in January, he urged middle powers to work together rather than negotiate separately with larger powers.
“When we only negotiate bilaterally with a hegemon, we negotiate from weakness. We accept what is offered,” Carney said at the time. “This is not sovereignty. It is the performance of sovereignty while accepting subordination.”
Canadian officials insist the European initiative is not solely an attempt to pressure Washington. Even so, the strained U.S.-Canada relationship provides unavoidable context for Ottawa’s accelerating pivot toward Europe.
Defense partnership is already expanding
Canada and the EU have moved beyond rhetoric in defense cooperation.
This year, Canada became the first non-European country to join the EU’s Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, defense initiative. The €150 billion program supports joint procurement and expansion of defense-industrial capacity, giving eligible Canadian companies opportunities to participate in European projects.
Closer cooperation could extend to Arctic security, where Canada and European NATO members face Russian military activity, Chinese interest in northern shipping routes, and competition over resources and infrastructure.
Von der Leyen also proposed greater coordination on critical minerals and battery production. Canada possesses large reserves of minerals needed for defense equipment, electric vehicles, semiconductors, and advanced technology, while Europe is trying to reduce its dependence on China for strategic supply chains.
The combination makes Canada an attractive partner even if the two sides never create a formal associate-membership category.
Difficult negotiations lie ahead
Political enthusiasm in Strasbourg does not guarantee agreement among the EU’s 27 national governments.
Some European capitals may resist giving Canada access approaching single-market membership without requiring Ottawa to adopt EU regulations, accept judicial oversight, or open additional parts of its economy. Agricultural standards, provincial trade restrictions, digital regulation, and government procurement could become contentious.
Canada would also have to decide how much regulatory alignment it is prepared to accept. Greater access to Europe often comes with requirements to follow rules over which a nonmember has limited influence.
The proposal therefore presents a sovereignty tradeoff: Canada wants alternatives to dependence on the United States, but meaningful integration with Europe could require accepting European standards and institutional conditions.
Wednesday’s announcement opens negotiations rather than completes them. No treaty text has been released, no timetable for associate membership has been established, and neither the European Council nor European Parliament has approved a new status.
The October summit may show whether “associate membership” becomes a durable new model for cooperation between the EU and democratic partners outside Europe—or remains an ambitious political label for closer ties that Canada and Europe were already building.

sources.news_title: Canada and the EU: What ‘associate member’ status could mean
sources.text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said on Wednesday she wanted to open the door for Canada to become the European Union's first "associate member".
Earlier this week, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney — who was in Strasbourg to listen to von der Leyen's annual State of the Union address — said Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU but not membership.
WHAT MIGHT THE NEW RELATIONSHIP INVOLVE?
There is currently no such status as "associate member" set out in the European Union's treaties — though various versions of an associate-type of membership have been floated in the bloc over the years.
Most recently, Germany suggested Ukraine be an associate member as an interim stage to full accession, though the proposal failed to gain traction as some EU capitals pushed back.
WHAT IS CANADA SEEKING?
Carney is seeking new alliances amid repeated threats by U.S. President Donald Trump against Canada's sovereignty.
Both sides want to forge deeper cooperation to counter U.S. and Chinese economic dominance as well as preserve democracy and the rules-based international order, which they see as under threat.
In her speech, von der Leyen said the two sides would create a "common prosperity and economic space". This would include joint work on manufacturing, a tech alliance, integration of defence industrial bases, the Arctic, AI, energy and critical minerals.
WHY MIGHT THE IDEA OF 'ASSOCIATE MEMBER' BE COMPLICATED?
Implementing such an 'associate' status would be unprecedented and may be legally complex.
Von der Leyen was speaking in her capacity as President of the European Commission, the bloc's executive arm. It would fall on the EU member states to decide whether the idea flies.
There is no suggestion von der Leyen is proposing enshrining the status of 'associate member' in EU treaties. That would require unanimity among all 27 capitals and ratification by all domestically.
Canada and the EU already have a trade agreement, called CETA. More than a decade after the deal was struck and nine years since it provisionally entered into force, several EU countries still have not ratified it.
If Canada wishes to become locked into the EU's Single Market, Ottawa would need to reconcile Canada's norms and regulations to match EU law.
Canada would become a rule-taker with no say on policy if it entered the Single Market without full membership like Iceland, Norway, Switzerland and Liechtenstein who are members of the European Economic Area.
Canada's rules have historically been geared towards its biggest trade partner, the United States.
WHAT DOES THIS MEAN FOR EU CANDIDATE COUNTRIES?
The quest for a deeper alliance between Canada and the EU will not impact the path to accession for European candidate states -- but it may serve as an irritant if Canada is perceived to be getting special treatment.
Accession negotiations and aligning with EU norms is a long process that often requires candidate nations to push through politically sensitive reform.
Full membership can only be granted to European states and provides access to the bloc's €18 trillion ($20.77 trillion) Single Market, voting and representation, EU funding and legal recourse to the European Court of Justice.
Ukraine saw Germany's proposal for "associate membership" as "unfair" as Kyiv would participate but with no voting rights.
The EU has said it could admit new members as soon as 2030. Montenegro, Albania, Ukraine and Moldova are the most advanced among candidate countries.
